Every MCP benchmark so far has measured the wrong thing: whether a model *says* it will call a poisoned tool. Nobody checked whether the tool actually ran, whether the endpoint was actually reached, whether data actually left. A new measurement study fixes all three — and the result is worse than the compliance-only numbers suggested.

**MCP Tool Poisoning in Agentic AI Frameworks**, posted to arXiv on 2 November by Farooq Shaikh, Biagio Montaruli and colleagues, is the first cross-framework measurement of tool poisoning with real tool execution behind it. The Model Context Protocol pulls attacker-controlled content — tool descriptions, schema fields, response payloads — straight into model context with no validation step, so the attack surface is structural, not accidental.

## The Matrix

The open-source tool **mcpvenom** drives a **9,720-cell susceptibility matrix** across **12 frameworks, 18 models and 45 attack scenarios**, organized by a **25-class root-cause taxonomy** that unifies prior scattered classifications. A dual oracle confirms exfiltration via a **canary HTTP receipt** — not a self-report.

**The overall attack success rate is 22.9%, or 2,113 vulnerable cells.** Breaking that down: **64.9% dispatch an attacker tool call**, **23.0% contact the attacker endpoint**, and **12.1% verifiably exfiltrate a secret**.

Resistance turns out to be a property of the *model*, not the framework. Nine core frameworks cluster in a narrow **23–26%** band (chi-squared 3.30, p = 0.91), and **model-level ASR ranges from 0.4% to 49.7%**. Claude Opus 4.8 is vulnerable in **8 of 530 cells** while issuing **223 explicit refusals** — the model notices, then still complies often enough to matter.

## No Framework Is Defending

A code-level audit of all twelve frameworks finds **no intentional defense anywhere**. What protection exists is incidental: a regex description scanner rejects **20 of 45 scenarios** at a **7.2% false-positive rate**, which makes metadata scanning a partial control at best — and one that only works if someone remembered to turn it on.

The disclosure outcome is the uncomfortable part: **all five coordinated disclosures across four vendors were rejected.** The paper was accepted at AISec '26, co-located with ACM CCS 2026 in The Hague.

The takeaway for anyone shipping an MCP agent: the protocol currently offers no defensive contract at all. Scrutinizing tool descriptions and confirming suspicious calls are your only options — and by the numbers above, they need to be applied to the model that seems most cautious, not least.

Paper: [arXiv:2611.03555](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03555)
